planting.note: Sow fresh seed in late summer or fall since germination is improved by a period of cold; plant in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or under deciduous trees.

directions: Perfoliate alexanders is a short-lived biennial umbellifer grown for the luminous chartreuse-green bracts that surround its small yellow flower umbels in late spring, giving the whole plant a glowing lime-green haze. In its first year it forms an unremarkable rosette of broad, three-lobed leaves; in its second year it bolts to two to three feet, flowers, sets seed, and dies, so a planting is best kept going by letting some seed drop each year to maintain a succession of ages. It is most effective massed under deciduous trees or at a woodland edge, where the acid-green color reads as a shot of light against darker foliage and pairs well with spring bulbs and emerging ferns. Sow fresh seed in late summer or fall, since seed loses viability quickly if stored dry, and keep the soil humus-rich and reliably moist through spring.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; wild garlic tolerates heat and drought once established.

directions: Wild garlic is a smaller, more strongly scented relative of the familiar society garlic, forming tight tufts of narrow, grayish, strap-shaped leaves that release a pungent garlic odor when brushed or crushed. In summer it sends up slender stems topped with small umbels of starry, pale lilac to greenish-white flowers that are valued more for the plant's long history as a flavoring and traditional remedy in southern Africa than for floral display. It spreads gradually from a cluster of fleshy rhizomes and is best grown in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, where it shrugs off heat and drought once established. Because it is less showy than its violet-flowered cousin, it suits an herb garden or a collector's bed of South African bulbs more than a border meant for color.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck near the soil surface in moist, well-drained soil in bright light with some protection from the hottest midday sun.

directions: Fire lily is a compact, clump-forming Cyrtanthus valued for its clusters of narrow, curved, bright orange-red tubular flowers held just above evergreen, strap-shaped foliage in summer. Unlike the large, solitary-flowered Scarborough lily (C. elatus), it produces several smaller flowers per umbel on a shorter stem, giving a neat, floriferous display well suited to pots and small border spaces. It grows from a narrow-necked bulb that resents being planted too deep and prefers reliably moist but free-draining soil through the growing season, with bright light tempered by some shade from the harshest sun. Where winters are too cold to leave it in the ground, it adapts readily to container culture and can be moved under cover for the winter months.

planting.note: Plant the bulb with its neck at or just above the soil surface in very free-draining, gritty soil in full sun to light shade, and allow a distinct dry rest after flowering.

directions: This grassland relative of the better-known Haemanthus albiflos and H. coccineus grows two broad, flat leaves that lie almost pressed to the ground rather than standing upright, suited to the open, seasonally dry grassland habitats of its native South Africa. In late summer to autumn, as the leaves are dying back, a short, dense, brush-like head of small pink to white flowers emerges directly from the bare bulb at ground level, giving the plant its paintbrush-like appearance. Because it follows a genuine dry dormancy tied to its grassland rainfall cycle, it needs a distinct dry rest after flowering rather than the steady moisture suited to more forest-adapted Haemanthus species. Grow it in very free-draining, gritty soil in full sun to light shade and treat it as a collector's bulb for a bright windowsill or alpine-style planting rather than a routine garden subject.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in fall; withhold water once foliage yellows in late spring to respect the summer-dormant Cape bulb cycle.

directions: The least commonly grown of the three cultivated cornflags, this South African corm produces the same fans of pleated, sword-shaped leaves as C. aethiopica and C. floribunda but is distinguished by its two-toned flowers, with a burnt-orange tube opening to a contrasting yellow lip, giving the arching winter flower spikes a brighter, more jewel-like look than its all-orange relatives. It follows the same winter-growing, summer-dormant rhythm typical of Cape bulbs, sending up fresh leaves with the autumn rains and flowering in late winter before going dormant through summer. Plant corms in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and withhold water once the foliage begins to yellow in late spring. It multiplies steadily from cormlets and is best used in a bulb border or naturalized drift where its bicolor flowers can be appreciated up close.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
